extracted.intended_audience: OSHA stakeholders, employers, occupational health and safety professionals, clinicians, and public commenters on heat-related workplace protections
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of scientific, medical, and practice-based definitions, diagnostic thresholds, treatment, recovery, surveillance, and return-to-work guidance for heat-related illnesses in workers used to support OSHA rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exertional heat stroke (EHS) — urgency of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat stroke must be treated as soon as possible and prolonged time between experiencing heat stroke and seeking treatment increases the likelihood of death and may result in long-term health effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA summary: physiological mechanisms are well established and heat exposure as a cause is well-recognized; treat immediately to reduce mortality and long-term sequelae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return-to-activity after exertional heat stroke (recommended timeframes)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACSM recommends a full return to activity between two to four weeks after the individual has demonstrated exercise acclimatization and heat tolerance with no abnormal symptoms or test results during the re-acclimatization period. National Athletic Trainers' Association proposes 7 to 21-day rest, asymptomatic, normal blood-work, and physician clearance prior to beginning a gradual return to activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military experience cautions that returning too early or without adequate work restrictions can cause incomplete recovery and prolonged restricted work status; data show 10-20% may have heat intolerance ~2 months post-event and some cases persist for months/years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat exhaustion — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH defines heat exhaustion as “[a] heat-related illness characterized by elevation of core body temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F) and abnormal performance of one or more organ systems, without injury to the central nervous system” (NIOSH, 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat exhaustion can progress to heat stroke if not treated properly and promptly; signs include profuse sweating, dizziness, nausea, headache, irritability, weakness, decreased urine output and core temperature up to 40 °C (104 °F). Significant CNS injury/inflammatory response do not occur during heat exhaustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat exhaustion — clinical management and triage
rubrics_metrics.description: When severity is unclear, treat the individual as if they have heat stroke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH recommended steps for a worker with heat exhaustion: take worker to clinic/ER for medical evaluation; if unavailable, call 911; someone should stay with worker; remove worker from hot area and give liquids; remove unnecessary clothing; cool with cold compresses or wash head/face/neck with cold water; encourage frequent sips of cool water. Armstrong et al. (1989) recommend rectal temperature to distinguish heat exhaustion vs heat stroke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat exhaustion — return-to-work restrictions and military protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat exhaustion may require restricted work status or limited duties for recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Donoghue et al. found 29% of miners required restricted work for at least one shift; AR 40-501: three instances of heat exhaustion in <24 months can prompt Medical Evaluation Board referral. Womack Army Medical Center permits mild cases to return to light duty next day and limited duty day after, but recommends avoiding strenuous exercise for several days and observation for delayed/subtle effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat syncope — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat syncope is defined as “fainting, dizziness, or light-headedness after standing or suddenly rising from a sitting/lying position” due to heat exposure (NIOSH, 2023a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called exercise-associated collapse sometimes, but heat syncope can occur without significant exertion; characterized by loss of consciousness (which is not required for exhaustion or stroke) and typically elevated skin temperature though not always elevated core temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat syncope — pathophysiologic mechanisms and differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two mechanisms: (1) reduced blood flow to the brain from vasodilation and decreased circulating volume causing fainting; (2) reduced cerebral blood velocity leading to orthostatic intolerance during heat stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate heat syncope from heat exhaustion and heat stroke: syncope always involves loss of consciousness and usually faster recovery of mental status; core temperature may not be elevated in syncope. Proper diagnosis requires ruling out other causes (cardiac, neurologic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat syncope — immediate treatment and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH recommends sit the worker in a cool environment and hydrate (water, juice, or sports drink).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department of the Army: victims recover rapidly once supine though complete recovery of stable BP and HR may take 1–2 hours. Athletes: lay supine with elevated legs to assist venous return, consider oral/IV rehydration. Episodes may require time away for evaluation; evaluate for injuries from falls and for cardiac/neurologic causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhabdomyolysis — definition and typical presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH: a medical condition associated with heat stress and prolonged physical exertion, resulting in rapid breakdown of muscle and necrosis of affected muscles (exertional rhabdomyolysis). Signs: myalgia, weakness, tenderness, swelling, dark-colored urine; onset may be delayed 24–72 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often co-occurs with exertional heat stroke, exhaustion, cramps, hyponatremia, and dehydration; recognized by NIOSH, Armed Forces, athletic bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhabdomyolysis — mechanisms of injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Two interrelated mechanisms: (1) thermal injury to muscle cells at high core temperatures (thermal maximum ≈ 107.6 °F / 42 °C) causing membrane breakdown and mitochondrial dysfunction; (2) ischemia to muscle cells from low blood volume and electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalemia) leading to muscle cell death during exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both mechanisms follow from excessive heat stress plus exertion and result in muscle breakdown and release of intracellular contents (CK, myoglobin) that cause complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhabdomyolysis — surveillance and case identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Armed Forces identify cases by searching medical records for ICD-10 codes for rhabdomyolysis and/or myoglobinuria plus other heat-related codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes military surveillance data show seasonal clustering (May–October) and a substantial proportion attributable to exertion/heat; surveillance approaches influence estimates of incidence in worker populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhabdomyolysis — treatment, monitoring, and complications
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment focuses on aggressive IV fluids (generally normal saline) to reduce CK and myoglobin and correct electrolytes; monitor CK repeatedly until a peak is reached and ensure CK trends downward before discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complications include hyperkalemia (arrhythmias) and myoglobin-induced nephrotoxicity leading to acute kidney injury; many cases require hospitalization with variable length (examples: mean 2.6–6 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhabdomyolysis — return-to-work guidance (military-derived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Military guidance: low-risk soldiers restricted to light, indoor duty and encouraged to rehydrate for ≥72 hours to allow CK normalization; if CK normalizes, progress to light outdoor duty ≥1 week then gradual return to full duty if no symptom recurrence; high-risk soldiers need additional diagnostics, expert consultation, and individualized restricted exercise programs prior to clearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes guidelines are limited outside military context and military protocols have been adopted/restated in surveillance reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyponatremia — definition and primary cause in heat exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyponatremia occurs when blood sodium <135 mEq/L and is often caused by excessive intake of water or hypotonic fluids without adequate sodium replacement during prolonged sweating/heat exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mild cases may be asymptomatic or cause dizziness, headache, nausea; severe cases can cause seizures, cerebral/pulmonary edema, coma, and be fatal. Heat exposure contributes by depleting sodium via sweat while high water intake dilutes serum sodium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyponatremia — treatment and clinical management
rubrics_metrics.description: Mild cases: increase salt intake (salty foods or oral hypertonic saline) and restrict fluids until symptoms resolve or sodium normalizes; severe cases require medical attention and may be life-threatening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider personal risk factors (heart conditions, low-sodium diets). Surveillance data (Armed Forces) document occurrences but diagnostic codes may include non-heat-related etiologies; controlling for comorbid diagnoses reduces overestimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat cramps — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH: heat cramps are “a heat-related illness characterized by spastic contractions of the voluntary muscles (mainly arms, hands, legs, and feet), usually associated with restricted salt intake and profuse sweating without significant body dehydration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat cramps may occur even with frequent water intake if electrolytes are not replenished; sometimes termed exercise-associated muscle cramps (EAMCs) but heat cramps are distinct to hot conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat cramps — proposed mechanisms and diagnostic criteria (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesized mechanism: profuse sweating depletes electrolytes (Na, K, Ca) exacerbating muscle fatigue and causing cramps. Early diagnostic criteria (Talbott & Michelsen, 1933) included exposure to high temperatures at work, painful muscle cramps, rapid salt loss in sweat not replaced, hypochloremia, and rapid symptom improvement after treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. Army notes intracellular calcium increase via reduced sodium gradient may drive actin-myosin contractions causing cramps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat cramps — treatment and return-to-activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment includes electrolyte-containing (isotonic) fluid replacement, stretching, massage, and in some cases sodium replacement; severe cases may need magnesium measurement/IV magnesium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACSM recommends rest, prolonged stretching, oral sodium chloride ingestion or IV normal saline in severe cases. NIOSH recommends medical attention if worker has heart problems, is on low-sodium diet, or cramps persist >1 hour. Most cases resolve and allow return to activity once symptoms subside; military guidelines may advise light/limited duty and avoiding strenuous exercise for several days in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic differentiation among heat illnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Different heat-related illnesses have overlapping features; differentiation is critical for correct treatment (e.g., rectal temperature recommended to distinguish heat exhaustion vs heat stroke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat syncope: always involves loss of consciousness but not necessarily elevated core temp; heat exhaustion and heat stroke do not require loss of consciousness; heat stroke is always characterized by markedly elevated core temperature and potential CNS injury; recovery speed differs (syncope recovers faster). When in doubt, treat as heat stroke.
